title: Traffic Noise May Raise Parkinson's Risk by 64 Percent, Dutch Study Finds
excerpt: A study of over 50,000 people in the Netherlands found that living with high levels of road traffic noise was independently associated with increased Parkinson's disease risk, adding to growing concerns about noise pollution as a neurological hazard.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • High road traffic noise exposure increases Parkinson's disease risk by 64%, according to a Dutch study of over 50,000 people.
  • Nitrogen oxide pollution is linked to more than double the risk of Parkinson's disease, independent of noise exposure.
  • A meta-analysis found a 10% increase in Parkinson's risk for every 5 μg/m³ rise in PM2.5 levels.
  • Indian cities exceed WHO noise limits, raising concerns about neurological impacts on millions living near heavy traffic.

The Dutch Evidence

Researchers at Utrecht University in the Netherlands analyzed data from two large population-based cohorts — the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC-NL) and the Occupational and Environmental Health Cohort Study (AMIGO) — covering 50,087 participants and 235 confirmed Parkinson's disease cases over up to 20 years of follow-up.

The results, published in the journal Environmental Epidemiology, showed a clear dose-response pattern. People living in the highest quartile of road traffic noise exposure (58 to 75 decibels, roughly the range between normal conversation volume and a vacuum cleaner) had 64% higher odds of developing Parkinson's compared to those in the quietest quartile (OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.13–2.43, p-trend = 0.005).

Nitrogen oxide exposure showed an even steeper gradient. Those in the highest NOx quartile had more than double the Parkinson's risk (OR 2.08, 95% CI 1.37–3.22). When both pollutants were analyzed together, NOx retained strong significance (OR 1.62), while noise remained elevated at OR 1.47 — suggesting each contributes independently to risk.

"Our results add to the existing evidence regarding air-pollutant exposures, in particular exposure to NOx, while additionally suggesting that road traffic noise may have an independent effect on PD development."

— Anke Huss, Institute for Risk Assessment Sciences, Utrecht University

A Growing Body of Global Research

The Dutch findings are not isolated. A UK Biobank study of 502,416 participants found that railway traffic noise was significantly associated with Parkinson's disease-related dementia (HR 1.042, 95% CI 1.005–1.081), while a 10-decibel increase in road noise raised Alzheimer's risk by 15%.

In July 2026, a Cambridge University meta-analysis published in Environment International pooled data from 26 Parkinson's studies and found that for every 5 μg/m³ increase in PM2.5 — fine particulate matter largely produced by traffic — the relative risk of Parkinson's rose by 10%. For PM10, each 15 μg/m³ increase raised risk by 18%.

"There are still relatively few robust studies that explore the link between air pollution and Parkinson's disease, but even so, it's becoming clear that there is a link," said Dr. Annalan Navaratnam, a clinical research fellow at Cambridge. "We urgently need more research, in larger populations, to examine what is a significant public health issue."

How Noise Damages the Brain

Research published in PLOS Biology by a team at Huazhong University of Science and Technology in China has begun to explain how noise affects the brain at a cellular level. Led by neuroscientist Pei Zhang, the team exposed a mouse model of pre-symptomatic Parkinson's to sound levels of 85 to 100 decibels — comparable to a busy restaurant or a revving motorcycle — for one hour per day over seven consecutive days.

While a single exposure caused temporary motor impairments that resolved within 24 hours, chronic exposure produced irreversible dopamine neuron loss in the substantia nigra, the brain region most affected in Parkinson's disease. The researchers identified a previously unknown neural circuit connecting the inferior colliculus (a sound-processing region) to the substantia nigra, and found that noise exposure significantly reduced expression of the VMAT2 gene, which is critical for dopamine transport.

When the team overexpressed VMAT2 in the presence of noise, it protected mice from both movement problems and neuron loss — pointing to a potential therapeutic pathway.

India's Noise Crisis and the Diaspora

The research carries particular weight for the Indian diaspora. According to the UN Environment Programme's 2022 Frontiers report, Indian cities are among the world's noisiest: Moradabad in Uttar Pradesh recorded 119 decibels, making it the second-loudest city globally after Dhaka. Delhi registered 83 dB, Kolkata and Asansol 89 dB each, and Jaipur 84 dB — all well above the WHO-recommended residential limit of 55 dB.

India's Central Pollution Control Board data shows Chennai averaging 67.8 dB during the day, with almost every Indian metro routinely violating national noise standards. The country's vehicle fleet surged from 55 million in 2001 to over 300 million by 2023, amplifying the noise and pollution problem in cities where millions live within meters of congested arterial roads.

For diaspora members who grew up in these environments, the cumulative exposure during formative years may be a relevant risk factor. The Dutch study assessed residential noise at baseline and followed participants for up to two decades — but early-life exposure in much louder environments like Indian cities may amplify risk further, though direct long-term studies in South Asian populations remain scarce.

What Comes Next

Parkinson's disease currently affects roughly 8.5 million people worldwide, with numbers projected to rise sharply as populations age. It has no cure, and its causes for most patients remain unknown — making identification of modifiable environmental risk factors particularly urgent.

The convergence of epidemiological evidence from European cohorts, mechanistic findings from laboratory research, and the meta-analytic confirmation of particulate matter links suggests that traffic-related exposures — both airborne pollutants and noise — deserve attention alongside established risk factors like pesticide exposure and genetics.

Cambridge researchers have created an open-access tool mapping over 1,000 policy interventions to reduce traffic emissions, including congestion charging, low-emission zones, and electric vehicle adoption. For cities like Delhi and Mumbai, where noise and air quality remain critical public health challenges, such measures may carry benefits beyond respiratory health — potentially helping protect the aging brain as well.
